slides.title: Meet the jellyfish
slides.newHtml:
Meet the jellyfish

Over 2,000 species worldwide — around for >600 million years
Simple animals — yet thriving in Earth’s oceans
  • No brain, heart, blood or bones — around 95% water
  • Stinging tentacles catch small fish (and even other jellyfish)
  • Nerve net coordinates responses; some glow in the dark
  • Numbers are increasing in warmer, more acidic oceans

slides.title: Exam question: are jellyfish alive? [3]
slides.oldHtml:
Exam question: are jellyfish alive? [3]

Jellyfish swim by rhythmic pulsations of the umbrella … usually feed on small fish … take oxygen into their cells directly from the water … have a nerve net which can coordinate responses … release sperm or eggs into the water.
Give 3 pieces of evidence that jellyfish are living.
swim → movement · feed → nutrition · sperm and eggs → reproduction · oxygen → respiration · nerve net → control
slides.newHtml:
Exam question: are jellyfish alive? [3]

Read the passage

Jellyfish swim by pulsing their umbrella-shaped bell and feed on small fish caught in their stinging tentacles.

They absorb oxygen directly from the water and have a nerve net that coordinates responses.

Most jellyfish release sperm or eggs directly into the water.

Suggest and explain 3 pieces of evidence that jellyfish are living.
  • Swim → movement
  • Feed on small fish → nutrition
  • Take in oxygen → respiration
  • Nerve net coordinates responses → sensitivity / control
  • Release sperm and eggs → reproduction

slides.title: Food tests: lab tips for clear results
slides.newHtml:
Food tests: lab tips for clear results

PREP FIRST: Crush solid foods with ~5–10 cm³ water (let bits settle or filter) — use only ~2 cm³ per tube — avoid dark foods (e.g. beetroot, soy sauce) that hide colours — keep glassware clean
Starch — Iodine
  • Use a white spotting tile so blue-black stands out
  • Only 2–3 drops of iodine on a tiny piece or drop — instant
  • Best foods: potato, bread, rice, pasta (not sugar!)
Glucose — Benedict’s
  • Equal volumes: ~2 cm³ food + ~2 cm³ Benedict’s
  • Heat in a ~80 °C water bath for 5 min (no direct Bunsen)
  • Best foods: apple juice, honey, onion (not table sucrose!)
Protein — Biuret
  • Add ~2 cm³ biuret to ~2 cm³ sample, shake gently (no heat)
  • Hold against white paper — weak positives are pale lilac
  • Best foods: egg white, milk, tofu, grated cheese
Lipids — Emulsion
  • Ethanol first (~2 cm³) + tiny smear, shake hard to dissolve fat
  • Then pour into ~2 cm³ cold water (keep ethanol off flames!)
  • Best foods: cooking oil, butter, crushed nut or sunflower seed

slides.title: Two kinds of covalent structure
slides.newHtml:
Two kinds of covalent structure

Sharing electrons can build either tiny separate molecules or one giant network
Simple molecular
  • Small, separate molecules (e.g. H₂O, CO₂, CH₄)
  • Weak forces between molecules → low m.p. & b.p.
Giant covalent
  • Millions of atoms bonded together (e.g. diamond, graphite, SiO₂)
  • Strong covalent bonds throughout → very high m.p. & b.p.

slides.title: Simple molecules
slides.oldHtml:
Simple molecules

Strong bonds inside
Weak forces between
Boiling breaks only the weak forces
→ low melting & boiling points
slides.newHtml:
Simple molecules

Two very different strengths of force:
  • Strong covalent bonds inside each molecule
  • Weak intermolecular forces between molecules
  • Boiling breaks only the weak forces
  • Low melting & boiling points

slides.title: Intermolecular forces in water
slides.newHtml:
Intermolecular forces in water

Inside each H₂O
Strong covalent bonds hold H and O together — these do not break when water boils
Dotted lines between H₂O
Weak intermolecular forces pull molecules together — boiling only overcomes these

slides.title: Do covalent substances conduct?
slides.oldHtml:
Do covalent substances conduct?

Usually no.
No ions and no free electrons to carry charge.
Exception: graphite (coming up…)
slides.newHtml:
Do covalent substances conduct?

Usually no
  • Molecules have no overall charge
  • No mobile ions or free electrons
  • Exception: graphite (delocalised e⁻)
  • Click substances to test!

slides.title: Bigger molecule → higher boiling point
slides.oldHtml:
Bigger molecule → higher boiling point

More intermolecular forces to overcome
slides.newHtml:
Bigger molecule → higher boiling point

Longer chains have stronger intermolecular forces between molecules, so more energy is needed to separate them

slides.title: Giant covalent structures
slides.oldHtml:
Giant covalent

A lattice of MANY strong covalent bonds
→ very high melting point
→ insoluble
→ don't conduct (except graphite)
slides.newHtml:
Giant covalent structures

Millions of non-metal atoms joined by strong covalent bonds
  • Like a giant ionic lattice, but with no charged ions
  • Very high melting & boiling points (lots of energy to break bonds)
  • Insoluble in water — no conduction (except graphite)
Why is Carbon so good at this?
Carbon (Group 4) has 4 outer electrons → forms up to 4 strong covalent bonds in every direction to build giant networks! (Silicon does too, e.g. quartz SiO₂.)
Each carbon shares electrons with 4 neighbours
Quartz (SiO₂) — giant covalent too

slides.title: Diamond
slides.newHtml:
Diamond

A giant 3D tetrahedral network of carbon atoms
  • Each carbon forms 4 strong covalent bonds to 4 other carbons
  • Extremely hard — rigid 3D lattice in every direction
  • Very high melting point (above 3550 °C) — lots of energy needed to break strong bonds
  • Does not conduct electricity — no delocalised electrons
  • Uses: jewellery, industrial cutting blades & drill tips
Rough & cut diamonds (Smithsonian, Public Domain)

slides.title: Graphite
slides.newHtml:
Graphite

Flat hexagonal layers of carbon atoms
  • Each carbon forms 3 strong covalent bonds (leaving 1 free electron per atom)
  • Soft & slippery — only weak forces between layers, so sheets slide over one another
  • Conducts electricity — delocalised electrons move freely along layers
  • Very high melting point (~3650 °C) — strong bonds within each sheet
  • Uses: pencil lead, solid lubricants, electrodes
Graphite
Pencil lead

slides.title: Fullerenes (e.g. C60)
slides.newHtml:
Fullerenes (e.g. C60)

Hollow simple covalent molecules of carbon
  • C60 (buckminsterfullerene): hollow ball of 60 carbon atoms — a buckyball
  • Separate molecules held by weak intermolecular forces → soft, slide/roll easily, lower m.p. than diamond
  • Does not conduct electricity — electrons cannot jump between separate C60 molecules
  • Huge surface area & hollow interior (plus nanotubes!)
  • Uses: lubricants, catalysts, targeted drug delivery

Distance and time must be in the units the answer needs:

slides.title: Worked example: Mercury
slides.newHtml:
Worked example: Mercury

Mercury takes 87.97 days to orbit the Sun. Its orbital radius is 57.91 million km. Find its speed.
distance = 2 × π × 57.91 million km = 363.9 million km
speed = 363.9 million ÷ 87.97 = 4.14 million km/day
in m/s: 4 140 000 000 m ÷ 86 400 s = 47 900 m/s

slides.title: Learning pit stop

Learning pit stop

Your turn: use v = 2πr ÷ T. Click to check each answer.
1. A rock on a string is swung round in a circle of radius 1.2 m. One turn takes 0.5 s. Find its orbital speed.
→ 2 × π × 1.2 ÷ 0.5 = 15.1 m/s
2. The Moon orbits the Earth in 27 days. Its orbital radius is 362 600 km. Find its orbital speed.
→ 2 × π × 362 600 ÷ 27 = 84 400 km/day (977 m/s)
3. A woman stands on the equator. The Earth's radius is 6371 km and it turns once in 24 hours. How fast is she moving?
→ 2 × π × 6 371 000 ÷ 86 400 = 463 m/s
